metadata.title: The socio-familiar context and its impact on student reading performance in PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata and draws an analytic sample via random sampling within each of the six specified countries (n=5,000 per country). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or software that would automatically apply them. Because the analyses are multilevel and logistic regression based on SPSS, the paper’s weighting approach is unclear; therefore, readers should treat the reported predictive proportions (e.g., ~20% and ~15%) as descriptive/predictive associations rather than fully population-representative estimates. For replication with PISA Data, analysts should apply the official student sampling weights and, if available, replicate weights to respect the complex survey design and nested structure (students within schools within countries).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is reading performance from PISA 2015, but the paper does not describe how missing responses were handled (e.g., complete-case exclusion vs. imputation) or how PISA plausible values were combined in the multilevel and logistic regression analyses. This is a reporting gap because PISA typically includes missingness and uses plausible values for achievement scales; without documentation, it is not possible to verify whether missing data were excluded or imputed and whether PVs were properly propagated through the models. Consequently, the reported predictive percentages and significance tests may be sensitive to the (undocumented) missing-data and PV-combination choices.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants are recruited from the PISA 2015 databases and selected based on students’ mother tongue (Spanish or English). The study restricts the dataset to six OECD countries/economies: Spain, Chile, Uruguay (Spanish-speaking block) and Great Britain, United States, Ireland (English-speaking block). The authors further apply two inclusion criteria in the selection process: (1) official language Spanish/English and (2) OECD membership and/or among the highest average performance in PISA 2015 reading. For analysis, students are randomly sampled within each nation (n=5,000 students per country), and reading performance is operationalized using the PISA 2015 reading test items (10 items) and an overall summation score; social/family predictors are recoded from questionnaire scales into nominal yes/no categories for logistic regression.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Reading (students aged 16; mother tongue: Spanish vs English; 6 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading performance (overall score; PV-based reading literacy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel analysis: socio-family variables explain ~20% of reading performance variability in Spanish-speaking countries and ~15% in English-speaking countries. Binary logistic regression: parental education predicts optimal and poor reading profiles; educational role variables (interest/support) predict optimal profiles in English-speaking countries (reported p-values include p=.001 and p=.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Reading the study leveraged parental education level and parents’ educational-role indicators (interest in school activities and support for academic efforts) to predict students’ reading performance profiles, finding that the socio-familiar context explains about 20% of reading performance variability in Spanish-speaking countries and about 15% in English-speaking countries. This indicates that strengthening parental educational involvement and support—especially around school activities—may be a practical lever for improving reading outcomes, though the study’s multilevel/logistic approach does not establish causal effects and the PV/missing-data handling is not fully documented.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2015 reading performance among 30,000 16-year-old students selected by mother tongue (Spanish vs English) across six countries: Spain, Chile, Uruguay, Great Britain, United States, and Ireland. The authors use multilevel analysis and binary logistic regression in SPSS, treating reading performance as a dependent variable derived from 10 reading items and an overall summation, and recoding parental education/occupation and parental educational-role items into nominal predictors. Results indicate that the socio-familiar context predicts roughly 20% of reading performance variability in Spanish-speaking countries and 15% in English-speaking countries, with the strongest incidence attributed to average parental education and parents’ interest in school activities and educational support. The paper reports significant differences between language blocks and provides p-values and model fit statistics (e.g., R² ranges in multilevel models and omnibus/Wald tests in logistic regression). Limitations include lack of documented plausible-value combination and missing-data strategy, and the absence of explicit survey-weight handling details, which constrains interpretability for population-level inference.
